publisher: Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability, Duke University
title: Flexibility Will Go a Long Way Toward Managing the Grid of the Near Future, Researchers Say (data-centre flexibility report by Martin Ross and Jackson Ewing)
date_evidence: duke-study-data-center-load-flexibility-us-150b-savings-feb-2026 ... The new follow-up report was released on February 17, 2026 by Duke University's Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability. Authors Martin Ross and Jackson Ewing ... savings ... range from $40 billion to $150 billion over the next decade ... 5 to 10 years
key_claim: A February 2026 Nicholas Institute (Duke) analysis by Martin Ross and Jackson Ewing models the economics of large data-centre load flexibility over a 5-to-10-year horizon and finds electricity-system savings (avoided capital, operating and fuel costs) ranging from $40 billion to $150 billion over the next decade across most modelled scenarios, with flexible large loads able to be integrated using existing grid headroom rather than waiting on new build.
frame_summary: Argues that allowing large data-centre loads to flex during peak hours is economically superior to building new generation and grid for them, saving the system $40-150 billion over the decade and converting a supply problem into a demand-flexibility opportunity.
verbatim_quote: $40 billion to $150 billion over the next decade
notes: Tier 2 structural anchor (17 Feb 2026, ~4 months): the canonical primary economic case for the flexibility-as-headroom thesis. One anchor permitted.

title: FERC to Act on Large Load Interconnection Docket by June 2026 (Docket No. RM26-4-000)
date_evidence: FERC to Act on Large Load Interconnection Docket by June 2026 ... April 16, 2026 ... This page was last updated on April 16, 2026
key_claim: On 16 April 2026 FERC said it will act by June 2026 on the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Docket RM26-4-000), initiated at the US Secretary of Energy's October 2025 direction, to reform how large loads (generally above 20 MW) such as data centres interconnect; the ANOPR asks whether large and co-located loads that agree to be flexible and curtailable should move through interconnection studies faster (potentially within 60 days), and FERC staff reviewed over 3,500 pages of comments, having already issued a December 2025 order on PJM co-located load and approved Southwest Power Pool's High Impact Large Load initiative in January 2026.
frame_summary: Argues that the federal interconnection regime is being rewritten to give flexible, curtailable large loads a faster path onto the grid, making curtailability an explicit regulatory lever for managing data-centre demand.
notes: Tier 1; the US federal regulatory core of the signal - a flexible/curtailable interconnection fast lane.

title: 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment
date_evidence: NERC's annual summer assessment, published May 19, 2026 ... In ERCOT, NERC reduced its 2026 summer forecast for total internal demand by 1.9 GW, or 2.3% ... NERC dropped its forecast for net internal demand by 3.7 GW, or 4.6%, because more data centers can be curtailed ... Texas law requires loads of 75 MW or more that interconnect from 2026 onwards to accept mandatory curtailment
key_claim: NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment (published 19 May 2026) cut its ERCOT total-internal-demand forecast by 1.9 GW (2.3%) and its net-internal-demand forecast by 3.7 GW (4.6%) to reflect that more data centres can now be curtailed by grid operators during emergencies; Texas law requires large loads of 75 MW or more interconnecting from 2026 onwards to accept mandatory curtailment during firm load-shed events.
frame_summary: Argues that curtailable data-centre load is no longer hypothetical but is already changing official reliability forecasts, with mandatory curtailment now written into Texas interconnection law.
notes: Tier 1; hard evidence the signal is landing - reliability forecasts now credit curtailable load, and Texas mandates it.

title: DCFlex: Data Center Flexible Load Initiative
date_evidence: DCFlex: Data Center Flexible Load Initiative - ongoing EPRI research initiative program page, no single article publication date; accessed 2026-06-16. EPRI's DCFlex program works with hyperscalers and utilities on protocols for large-load demand response; demonstrations have shown roughly 25% data-centre load reduction without service interruption and a reference design that could unlock about 100 GW of grid capacity.
key_claim: EPRI's DCFlex initiative, a multi-party programme spanning demonstration sites across the US and Europe, develops the protocols, measurement standards and contractual arrangements to make large-load demand response a routine grid service; field demonstrations have shown roughly 25% data-centre load reduction sustained during grid stress without interrupting AI service, and a resulting reference design could unlock on the order of 100 GW of grid capacity nationally.
frame_summary: Argues that data-centre flexibility is technically real and reproducible - a 25% curtailment without service loss - and can be standardised into a routine grid service rather than a one-off pilot.
notes: Tier 2 research institute; evergreen program page used for the capability-proof framing (25% curtailment, ~100 GW reference design).

title: How load flexibility buys time for America's data center boom (ICF authors Shanthi Muthiah and Himali Parmar)
date_evidence: How load flexibility buys time for America's data center boom ... was published on Utility Dive on June 9, 2026 ... when load flexibility is layered as a tool, PJM can reliably absorb an additional 30 GW without further new generation ... Public Service Co. of Oklahoma's program procured capacity at $32/kW-year (versus $100+/kW-year for BTM generation
key_claim: A 9 June 2026 Utility Dive analysis by ICF energy strategists argues that in supply-constrained markets grid connection now comes with a choice - bring your own power, or bring flexibility - and that when flexibility is layered as a tool PJM can reliably absorb an additional 30 GW without new generation; retail demand response can be far cheaper than self-supply, with Public Service Co. of Oklahoma procuring capacity at $32/kW-year versus $100+/kW-year for behind-the-meter generation at a data centre.
frame_summary: Argues that load flexibility is becoming the practical alternative to new generation for getting data centres connected, and is cheaper than behind-the-meter self-supply, reframing grid access as a flexibility bargain.
notes: Tier 3 trade analysis; the market reframing - bring power or bring flexibility - and the cost comparison.

title: Spring 2026 update on further Demand Connection Reform for Data Centres and other Large Energy Users
date_evidence: Spring 2026 update on further Demand Connection Reform for Data Centres ... The article was published on March 18, 2026 ... DESNZ is considering whether some categories of very large demand users, such as datacentres, should be required to provide a mandatory minimum level of demand flexibility ... 81% of data centre projects would accept non-firm, ramped, or phased connections for an earlier date
key_claim: A 18 March 2026 CMS briefing on Great Britain's demand-connection reform reports that DESNZ is considering requiring some very large demand users, such as data centres, to provide a mandatory minimum level of demand flexibility so the system operator can curtail or limit them during network or system stress, and that 81% of data-centre projects would accept non-firm, ramped or phased connections in exchange for an earlier connection date, against a connections queue dominated by roughly 50 GW of data-centre demand.
frame_summary: Argues that Britain is moving the same direction as the US - conditioning data-centre grid connections on flexibility and non-firm terms - with mandatory minimum flexibility under active consideration.
notes: Tier 3 law-firm briefing; the UK transatlantic dimension - DESNZ mandatory-flexibility proposal and non-firm connections.

title: More than 75 data center build-outs worth $130 billion have been blocked in 2026 as bipartisan opposition mounts
date_evidence: More than 75 data center build-outs worth $130 billion have been successfully blocked in the first four months of 2026 - bipartisan opposition mounts nationwide over fears of soaring power and water costs
key_claim: More than 75 data-centre build-outs worth about $130 billion were blocked or stalled in the first months of 2026 amid bipartisan local opposition over rising power and water costs, indicating the data-centre demand the flexibility debate assumes is itself contested and politically constrained.
frame_summary: Argues that the data-centre boom faces mounting community and political resistance over cost and water, casting doubt on whether the demand premise behind the flexibility debate will fully materialise.
notes: Tier 3; the counter-argument evidence - the demand premise behind flexibility is contested by local opposition.
